prize_parts.citation: For the optical lattice clock, from the magic-wavelength trapping concept to comparisons between independent clocks at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I have changed my preferred configuration from B051 (Kane, Molenkamp, Hasan) to the optical lattice clock, B015, with Katori and Ye. The reason is mainly the credit problem I flagged in round 1, which the exchange did not resolve. Mehlig pointed out that Kane and Mele are one theory partnership and that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal guided Molenkamp's experiment, so any trio from the credited names leaves out a decisive contributor, and no one proposed a way to split Kane from Mele that I can defend. A discovery whose physics I trust but whose allocation I cannot defend is not a good final position. On B015, the round-1 discussion changed my view of the science as well. Kroll, Lindroth and Mehlig argued that the magic-wavelength lattice removes the trade-off between the number of interrogated atoms and freedom from Doppler and recoil shifts, which is a conceptual step beyond the ion clocks of 2012 and the comb of 2005, and not only a tighter number. That is a physical principle, and it is the kind of reasoning I accept. The result also meets my own tests of robustness: independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST and SYRTE agree at the 10^-18 level, the systematic shifts (blackbody, lattice light shifts, many-body interactions) are understood quantitatively, and the clocks have already measured gravitational redshift at the millimetre scale and bounded drifts of constants. The credit is a clean pair, Katori for the scheme and Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability. I would ask that the citation name the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 regime and leave the unfinished redefinition of the second out.
statement.case_against: My earlier reservations about B015 remain and I do not want to hide them. It is a measurement advance, not the discovery of a new state of matter, and a purist can ask whether it fits the statutory emphasis on discovery or invention better than B051 or B017. The 2005 and 2012 prizes are adjacent, so the citation must carry the novelty argument, and if it reads as 'a better clock' it rewards degree more than kind. A two-name credit also cannot reflect the contributions of Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups. Finally, B051 remains in my view the stronger discovery in the physical sense, with fifteen years of independent transport and ARPES confirmation, and if the committee could settle the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp-Hasan allocation I would reconsider.

responses.point: Mehlig disputed that the B051 allocation is nearly settled: Kane and Mele are a single theory partnership, the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal guided the HgTe experiment, and Zhang is deceased, so any trio from the credited names omits a decisive contributor.
responses.response: He is right, and this is the main reason I moved. The chair asked whether Mele can be separated from Kane, and I cannot give a principled answer. His trio (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) drops Hasan, whose ARPES work established the three-dimensional case, and mine drops Mele, so the two trios show the problem without fixing it. I therefore no longer prefer B051 as a final position, and I keep it as an alternative because I think the physics is sound. On B015, I accept his view that the citation should name the mechanism and not only the number 10^-18, and that the redefinition of the second should stay out.

responses.point: Kroll argued that the magic-wavelength lattice is a new principle for clock operation, interrogating a large ensemble with Doppler and recoil effects removed, which neither the 2005 comb prize nor the 2012 single-ion prize covers, and that the pending SI redefinition is timing only.
responses.response: This persuaded me on the point I was most unsure of in round 1. I had treated the lattice clock as a large quantitative step on the ion clocks, and the many-atom statistical advantage is a real difference in kind. I agree that the 10^-18 comparisons between independent laboratories are already in hand, so I would not wait for the redefinition. I note his Boulder background and his request that it be recorded, and I think it should be, but I see no bearing on the credit of Katori and Ye. On the drafting question, I would write the citation around the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 regime, as he suggests.

responses.point: Lindroth said the physics at the 1e-18 level needed the magic-wavelength condition, control of blackbody and lattice light shifts, and many-body interactions in a degenerate Fermi gas, and raised whether Katori and Ye alone represent the field and which second part, if any, would fit.
responses.response: Her point that the 10^-18 level required understanding of blackbody, lattice light shifts and many-body interactions is what a theorist wants to hear, because it means the result is understood and not only measured. On whether two names are enough, I do not see a defensible third name: Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke and Ludlow all contributed but no one has proposed a better pair, and adding a third name would invite the same dispute I could not resolve for B051. I would say so in the citation record and accept that the pair is imperfect but still the cleanest on the shortlist. I do not think a second part is needed; I could not find one that is both distinct and fits the three-person limit.

responses.point: Olsson prefers magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B017) as a theory-plus-experiment door-opener reproduced by many groups, and accepts that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that the credit for Cao and the Dean, Young, Efetov and Yacoby groups is open.
responses.response: I share her interest in a graphene system producing new physics, and her honest list of open credits is the reason I keep B017 as an alternative and not a first choice. Reproduction across many groups is real, but the origin of the correlated states and the superconductivity is still debated, and twist-angle disorder makes sample dependence a concern, so I would rather wait for a settled interpretation. I am glad that she says she would not oppose B015, and I do not oppose B017 as a later candidate.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers a two-part prize pairing B015 with IceCube (B040, Halzen alone), valuing cases where nature supplied a clue and an instrument was built to read it, and concedes the single-name IceCube credit is the weak point.
responses.response: I agree with him on B015 and on his criterion, but I cannot support the second part. Astroparticle physics is far from my field, so I defer to him and Pearce on the science, but a single name for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and ANTARES behind it, is exactly the kind of credit problem that made me leave B051, and the source identifications are still developing. I would support B015 alone and I would be open to the neutrino case in a later cycle if a defensible credit can be written.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye alone adequately recognise the lattice clock given Lemonde, Pfau, Lemke, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups, with no alternative pair proposed.
Whether a precision-measurement achievement fits the statutory emphasis on discovery or invention better than a new state of matter such as B051, given the 2005 and 2012 prizes nearby.

Whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second or rest on demonstrated 10^-18 performance, which I currently favour, and whether the novelty relative to earlier prizes can be put in one citation sentence.
Whether my move away from B051 is only a reaction to an attribution problem that an expert report could resolve, for example on the Kane-Mele pairing and the HgTe proposal.
I rely on memory for the details of the independent clock comparisons and the early NIST and PTB lattice-clock demonstrations, and would welcome an external review.
statement.conflict_note: No known personal, collaborative or institutional tie to Katori, Ye, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan or any other shortlisted candidate. I chaired the 2025 committee, which bears on overlap arguments for circuit QED (B012) but is not a recusal issue. I note Kroll's disclosure of his year in John Hall's Boulder laboratory, and I have no similar tie to Jun Ye's group or to Katori. I have worked with Los Alamos and facility theory in electronic structure, which has no connection to optical clocks.
